blurb: The design inside every modern chatbot, explained from zero: how it reads, how attention works, and how it writes a reply.

cards.title: The problem transformers solved

steps.p: At heart, ChatGPT or Claude does one thing: given some text, predict the next word. Do that over and over and you get a reply. The transformer is the design that does the predicting.

steps.h: The old way: one word at a time
steps.p: Before 2017, language models (RNNs) read text strictly in order, carrying a running memory from word to word.
steps.analogy: Reading a book through a keyhole, keeping a mental summary as you go.

steps.p: Everything had to squeeze through that one running memory, so early words faded by the end of a long passage. And reading in order meant training couldn't be split up and done in parallel — so it was slow.

steps.h: Attention: look at everything at once
steps.p: Transformers let every word look directly at every other word, all at once. To understand "it" in "The cat sat because it was tired", the model can look straight back at "cat".
Because all words are processed at the same time, training spreads across thousands of GPU cores. That speed is what made today's giant models possible.

cards.aside: Transformers come from a 2017 Google paper, "Attention Is All You Need".

cards.q: The biggest practical reason transformers overtook older RNN models was that they…
options: Can process all the words of a training passage at the same time
Were invented by a bigger company
cards.hint: Keyhole reading vs seeing the whole page.
cards.why: Parallel processing. RNNs must finish word 1 before word 2. Transformers handle every word at once, so training uses GPUs fully and scales to huge datasets.

cards.statement: The original 2017 transformer was built for translating languages, not for chatbots.
cards.why: True. It was tested on English–German and English–French translation. Its use for chatbots came later.

cards.title: All eight authors of "Attention Is All You Need" are listed as equal contributors, in random order.
cards.detail: The paper's footnote says so. Nearly all of them later left Google to found or join AI companies, including Cohere and Character.AI.

cards.q: In "The cat sat because it was tired", how does a transformer work out what "it" means?
options: "it" looks directly at every earlier word and focuses on "cat"
It only looks at the word just before
cards.hint: Look at the cells in step 4.
cards.why: Attention. Every word can look at every other word and decide which matter most for understanding it.

cards.statement: Attention on its own knows the order of the words it's reading.
cards.hint: Looking at everything at once loses something.
cards.why: False. Attention sees all words at once, like a bag. Position information has to be added separately, or "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same.

steps.p: First, every word (token) is turned into a long list of numbers — a vector — that captures its meaning.
From each word's vector, the model makes three new ones: a query ("what am I looking for?"), a key ("what do I offer?") and a value ("what I'll pass on").
steps.analogy: A library: your query is your search, each book's key is its catalogue label, and its value is the contents.

steps.p: Each word's query is compared with every word's key. A good match gives a high score. "it" looking for a noun scores high with "cat".

visual.caption: How much "it" attends to each word. The percentages add to 100%.

steps.p: The scores become percentages adding to 100%. The word's new meaning is a blend of everyone's values, weighted by those percentages — mostly "cat".
A model runs many of these "attention heads" in parallel. One might track grammar, another who-did-what, another nearby words.

cards.q: In attention, what is a word's "query" for?
options: Describing what that word is looking for in other words
cards.why: What it's looking for. Queries are matched against other words' keys to decide where to pay attention.

cards.q: For one word, the attention percentages across all the other words add up to…
cards.why: 100%. Softmax turns raw scores into shares of a whole, so the result is a weighted average of values.

cards.q: Why have many attention heads instead of one?
options: Each head can track a different kind of relationship at the same time
Because one head can't do maths
cards.why: Different relationships. Grammar, meaning and references can each get their own head, working side by side.

cards.statement: In a GPT-style chatbot, a word can look at words that come after it.
cards.why: False. It can only look backwards. Otherwise, when learning to predict the next word, it could just peek at the answer.

cards.title: Researchers found a two-head pattern, called an induction head, that lets models copy patterns from earlier in a prompt.
cards.detail: One head finds where the current word appeared before; another copies what came next. Anthropic's 2022 work linked these to models learning from examples in a prompt.

cards.title: The block that repeats dozens of times

steps.p: A transformer is the same block repeated — dozens or even over a hundred times. Each block refines the understanding a bit more.
Attention lets words share information with each other — the "talking" step.
Then each word is processed on its own by a small neural network (the MLP). This is where much of the model's knowledge seems to be stored — and most of its parameters.
steps.analogy: Attention is a group discussion; the MLP is each person going away to think it over.

steps.p: Each part adds its result to the input rather than replacing it (a "residual" connection), and numbers are normalised to stay in a sensible range. This keeps deep stacks trainable.
Most modern models add position by rotating each word's vectors by an amount based on its position (RoPE), so attention can tell near from far.

cards.q: In a standard transformer block, which part holds most of the parameters?
cards.hint: The part where each word "goes away to think".
cards.why: The MLP. It's typically about two-thirds of a block's parameters, and research suggests much factual knowledge lives there.

cards.statement: Within a layer, every word position is processed with the same parameters.
cards.why: True. The same block is applied to every position. That's why one model can handle text of different lengths.

cards.title: The MLP layers seem to act like a memory for facts.
cards.detail: Research such as Geva et al. (2021) found that facts like "Eiffel Tower → Paris" are largely stored in MLP layers — and can even be edited there.

options: Adds each part's result to its input instead of replacing it
cards.why: Add, don't replace. Information and training signals can flow straight through many layers, which keeps very deep models trainable.

cards.statement: Most modern models normalise numbers before each part of the block, rather than after as in the 2017 paper.
cards.why: True. "Pre-norm" turned out to make training of very deep models much more stable.

cards.title: How a chatbot writes a reply

steps.h: Read the whole prompt at once
steps.p: Your entire message goes through the stack of blocks in one pass, all words in parallel.
At the end, the model gives a probability for every possible next token. One is picked.
That token is added to the text and the whole process runs again to pick the next one — one token per pass, until the reply is done.
GPT-style models predict the next word, so they're good at writing. BERT-style models fill in hidden words using both sides, so they're good at understanding and search.
The same design handles images (cut into patches), audio and video — almost all modern AI uses transformers.

options: Filling in hidden words using the words on both sides
cards.hint: Look at the comparison in step 4.
cards.why: Fill in the blanks. Seeing both sides makes it great at understanding, but it isn't built to write long text.

cards.statement: Vision transformers chop an image into small squares and treat each one like a word.
cards.why: True. A photo becomes a sequence of patch tokens, and the same attention machinery takes over.

cards.q: You double the length of the text. Roughly how does the attention work grow?
cards.hint: Every word compares with every other word.
cards.why: Quadruples. Twice the words means twice as many words each comparing with twice as many others: 2 × 2 = 4.

cards.title: FlashAttention made attention several times faster without changing its maths at all.
cards.detail: It computes exactly the same result in small tiles that stay in the GPU's fast on-chip memory, avoiding slow trips to main memory.

cards.title: Test your understanding by explaining it
cards.body: If you can explain attention in two sentences, you understand it.
cards.challenge: Explain to someone: how does a chatbot know what "it" refers to in a sentence?
